0.title: Who Jesus Is and What He Has Done
0.essay:
Jesus once asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” (Matthew 16:15). Everyone who has ever heard of him must answer the same question.

The question that matters most

Some say he was a good teacher, a prophet, a revolutionary or a legend. Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), and Jesus said that answer had come from the Father himself.

Christianity is not first a set of ideas or a way of life. It is a person. Take Christ out of Christianity and nothing is left. Everything the Bible says about salvation hangs on two questions: who is Jesus, and what has he done? If he is not God, he cannot save us. If he is not truly man, he cannot stand in our place. If he did not die for our sins, we are still in them. And “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17).

His person and his work

This study looks at both: the person of Christ, who he is, and the work of Christ, what he has done, is doing and will do. The two belong together. Only someone who is both God and man could do what Jesus did, and what he did shows us who he is. The aim is not only to understand Christ better but to love and trust him more.

The chapters

The Word Became Flesh; Truly God and Truly Man; Prophet, Priest and King; The Cross: Christ Our Substitute; Risen, Ascended and Reigning; and He Will Come Again.

1.title: The Word Became Flesh
1.essay:
John’s Gospel does not begin in Bethlehem. It begins before creation: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Before all things

John deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis. Before anything was created, the Word already was. He was “with God”, a distinct person from the Father. He “was God”, sharing the Father’s nature. And he was the Creator: “All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made” (John 1:3). Jesus is not the highest creature. He is the one through whom all creatures came to be.

So the Son did not become the Son at Bethlehem. He is the eternal Son of the eternal Father. On the night before he died he prayed, “And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5).

The most astonishing sentence

Then comes the most astonishing sentence ever written: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Two words carry the weight. He became flesh — real humanity, a real body and a real human soul. And he dwelt among us; the word means “pitched his tent”, like God’s presence in the tabernacle in the wilderness. The glory that once filled the tabernacle was now seen in a man. To see Jesus is to see God’s glory up close.

He did not stop being God. He did not merely appear human or borrow a body for a while. He became what he was not, while remaining what he was. This is the incarnation.

The virgin birth

Matthew and Luke both record that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of Mary, a virgin. Mary asked, “How will this be, since I am a virgin?” The angel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her, “therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God” (Luke 1:34–35). Gabriel’s message joined two lines of promise. Jesus would be given “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32): the long-promised King. And he would be called the Son of God: more than a king. Mary’s son is David’s son and God’s Son at once.

The virgin birth is not a decorative miracle. It marks Jesus as a new beginning, the second Adam, truly human through Mary, yet not simply one more child of Adam’s line. Salvation comes from above, not from human achievement.

Why he came

Scripture gives several answers. He came to reveal the Father: “No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). He came to save: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15). He came to share our nature so that he could die in our place and defeat death (Hebrews 2:14). And he came to be “a merciful and faithful high priest” who understands our weakness (Hebrews 2:17).

He emptied himself

Paul writes that Christ, “though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:6–7). The Lord of glory was born in a borrowed stable, grew up in an obscure town and worked with his hands. He went all the way down to death on a cross, the most shameful death the Roman world knew. Paul wrote this to stop quarrels in a church: if the Son of God made himself nothing for us, we can surely put others first.

Some modern teachers have read “emptied himself” to mean that the Son laid aside some of his divine attributes, such as his knowledge or power, so that on earth he was not fully God. Historic Christianity holds that he laid aside not his divine nature but his divine glory and privileges, by adding a human nature and taking the place of a servant. That is the right reading, because Paul himself explains how Christ emptied himself: “by taking the form of a servant”. The emptying was by addition, not subtraction. God cannot stop being God. Even on earth, Jesus calmed storms, forgave sins and knew people’s thoughts. Yet in his human nature he “increased in wisdom” (Luke 2:52), and by his own choice he lived in dependence on the Father and the Spirit.

God came near

The shepherds near Bethlehem were among the lowest of society. Yet the angels came to them, and the sign they were given was “a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger” (Luke 2:12). The Saviour of the world was announced to nobodies and found in a feeding trough.

A Christian who has always thought of Christmas as a sentimental holiday reads John 1:1–14 slowly in December. The baby in the nativity scene is the one through whom all things were made. Christmas stops being a pleasant festival and becomes a staggering fact: God came near.

When you picture Jesus, do you picture him as truly God, as truly man, or as both? Most of us lean one way. Scripture holds both.

For reflection

Read John 1:1–18. What does each verse tell you about who Jesus is? Why does it matter that he was born of a virgin? How would you explain Philippians 2:7 to someone who thinks Jesus gave up being God? Where is God calling you to imitate Christ’s humility this week?

2.title: Truly God and Truly Man
2.essay:
Who is Jesus? The New Testament answers with two truths that must never be separated: he is fully God and fully man, one person for ever.

Truly God

The New Testament calls Jesus God directly. Thomas had refused to believe without seeing the wounds. When Jesus offered them, Thomas made the highest confession in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Jesus did not correct him; he blessed those who would believe the same without seeing. Paul writes, “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9) — in his risen human body. The Colossians were being drawn to philosophies that promised something more, and Paul’s answer was that everything is already in Christ. There is nothing to add to him.

Jesus does what only God can do. He creates (Colossians 1:16), sustains the universe (Hebrews 1:3), forgives sins (Mark 2:5–7), raises the dead (John 5:21) and will judge the world (John 5:22). He receives worship (Matthew 14:33; Hebrews 1:6), which God gives to no creature. And he claims God’s own name: “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). His hearers understood him perfectly; they picked up stones to throw at him.

Truly man

Jesus was not God in disguise. He was born, grew up, learned, worked, ate, slept and got tired. He was thirsty at the well and wept at Lazarus’s tomb (John 4:6–7; 11:35). He felt sorrow, anger, compassion and joy. He was “in every respect … tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). He died a real death and was raised with a real body, which he still has.

His sinlessness does not make him less human. Sin is not part of what it means to be human; it is a corruption of it. Jesus is the truest human who ever lived.

One person

Jesus is not two persons, a divine one and a human one, sharing a body. He is one person, the eternal Son, with two natures. Whatever either nature does, the one person does. That is why Paul can say that the rulers “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). God did not die in his divine nature, which cannot die. But the one who died was God the Son, in his human nature.

In AD 451, at the Council of Chalcedon, the church summarised this biblical teaching. Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, “without confusion” (the natures are not blended into something new), “without change”, “without division” and “without separation”. That was not new teaching. It was a fence around the mystery the New Testament already reveals.

Why both matter

Only a man could die for men; only God could make that death of infinite worth and conquer death. Only a man could be our example and our sympathising priest; only God could be our Saviour and Lord. “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). The bridge must reach both banks.

So every error about Christ destroys salvation. Some, ancient and modern, deny that he is fully God and make him a created being, however exalted; Jehovah’s Witnesses teach this today. Others deny that he is fully human, making his body or his human mind an illusion. Others divide him into two persons, or blend his natures into a third thing. Each error removes either the God who saves or the man who stands in our place.

A sympathetic high priest

Why did the Son become human? To die, and by dying to destroy the devil’s power and free those enslaved by the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15). He had to be made like his brothers in every respect to be a merciful and faithful high priest, and “because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18).

Our high priest is great, for he has passed through the heavens; and he is sympathetic, for he was tempted as we are. That combination is why we can come boldly: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). We approach a throne, but it is a throne of grace, and the one beside it knows exactly what we face.

Asleep in the boat

In a storm on Galilee, Jesus was asleep in the boat, worn out like any man. Woken by terrified disciples, he spoke to the wind and sea, and there was a great calm. The disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). The same scene shows his true humanity and his true deity.

A Jehovah’s Witness couple knock on a Christian’s door and say that Jesus is “a god” but not God Almighty. Instead of arguing about a single verse, she opens John 20:28 and Hebrews 1:8–10 and asks, “If Jesus is not God, why does the Father call him God and Creator?” The conversation goes deeper than either side expected.

Do you bring your weaknesses to Jesus as someone who understands them? Do you worship him as someone who rules over them? Both are right.

For reflection

List three things Jesus did that only God can do, and three that show he was truly human. Why must our Saviour be both God and man? How does Hebrews 4:15–16 change the way you pray when you are tempted? How would you answer someone who says Jesus never claimed to be God?

3.title: Prophet, Priest and King
3.essay:
“Christ” is not Jesus’ surname. It means “anointed one”, the same as the Old Testament word Messiah. In Israel, three kinds of people were anointed or appointed to serve God: prophets, priests and kings. Jesus fulfils all three offices perfectly.

Christ the Prophet

At Sinai the people were terrified by God’s voice and asked for a mediator. God approved, and Moses promised, “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen” (Deuteronomy 18:15). The prophets who followed never fully fulfilled this; Deuteronomy itself ends by saying that no prophet like Moses had yet arisen (Deuteronomy 34:10). Jesus is that prophet (Acts 3:22).

But he is more than a prophet. The prophets brought God’s word; Jesus is God’s Word. “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). He is God’s final and complete word, and we listen to him in Scripture.

Christ the Priest

A priest represents people before God and offers sacrifice for their sins. Israel’s priests offered animals again and again, and then died and had to be replaced. Jesus is a better priest in every way. He offered not an animal but himself, and he offered once, not repeatedly: “he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27). He holds his priesthood permanently, “consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). He is both the priest and the sacrifice, and he never stops praying for his people.

Hebrews 1 shows the finished work: after “making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3). He sat down because his work was done. Every old priest “stands daily at his service” (Hebrews 10:11); there was always more to do. Because Christ is our one priest, Christians need no other priest to bring them to God and no repeated sacrifice. Every believer may come to God directly through him (Hebrews 10:19–22).

Christ the King

God promised David a son whose throne would last for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Jesus is that King. He was born “king of the Jews” (Matthew 2:2), entered Jerusalem on a donkey as Zechariah foretold, and was crucified under a sign naming him King. After his resurrection he said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). He reigns now at God’s right hand, ruling his church by his word and Spirit and ruling all things for its good (Ephesians 1:22).

Priest and king together

In Israel, priests came from the tribe of Levi and kings from Judah; no one could be both. But Psalm 110 foresees a King who is also a priest. David hears “The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1), and then, “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4), like the mysterious priest-king of Genesis 14. Jesus used this psalm to show that the Messiah is more than David’s son; he is David’s Lord (Matthew 22:41–45). Hebrews applies it to him (Hebrews 7).

Down and up

Christ carried out these offices in two stages. In his humiliation he was born in lowliness, lived under the law, suffered, died and was buried. In his exaltation he rose, ascended, sits at God’s right hand and will come to judge. Philippians 2:6–11 traces both: down to the cross, then up to the name above every name.

Our three needs

The three offices answer our three great needs. We are ignorant, and need a prophet to teach us. We are guilty, and need a priest to reconcile us. We are weak and enslaved, and need a king to rule and defend us. In Christ we have all three.

On the road to Emmaus, two disappointed disciples told the unrecognised Jesus that they had hoped he would redeem Israel. He answered, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” And “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:26–27). The whole Old Testament was pointing to him.

A believer is overwhelmed: confused about a decision, guilty over a sin, and anxious about forces beyond her control. Her pastor reminds her that Christ is her Prophet, guiding her through his word; her Priest, who has paid for her sin and prays for her now; and her King, who rules over everything she fears.

For reflection

Which of Christ’s three offices do you think about least, and why? Do you listen to him, rest in his sacrifice and submit to his rule? How does his ongoing intercession (Hebrews 7:25) encourage you? What would it look like to submit one area of your life to Christ as King this week?

4.title: The Cross: Christ Our Substitute
4.essay:
The cross is the centre of the Christian faith. The Gospels give a large share of their pages to the last week of Jesus’ life, and Paul said, “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2). But why did Jesus have to die?

Because of our sin

Sin is not merely a mistake or a weakness. It is rebellion against a holy God, and it deserves his just punishment. “For the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). No amount of good works can pay this debt, because even our best works are stained (Isaiah 64:6).

Because God loves

The cross was not an accident, nor a tragedy forced on God. It was planned before the world began (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:20). “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16). The Father did not have to be persuaded by the Son to love us. The cross is the expression of his love.

In our place

Isaiah saw it centuries before: “But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). Notice the contrast between “he” and “we”. We went astray; he was pierced. We had iniquities; he was crushed. We are healed; he was wounded. And above it all stands God’s own purpose: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

When James and John had just asked for the best seats in the kingdom, Jesus turned their ambition upside down. He came “not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45) — the price paid to free a captive, one dying in the place of the many. Peter, writing to slaves suffering unjustly, points them to Christ’s example, but cannot stop there: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). Paul says, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

The language is consistent. He took what we deserved, so that we could receive what he deserved. This is called penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty of sin as our substitute.

Many pictures, one heart

The New Testament uses many pictures for what the cross achieved. It is a sacrifice that removes guilt. It is propitiation, turning away God’s wrath (Romans 3:25). It is redemption, paying a ransom to free slaves. It is reconciliation, making enemies friends. It is victory: God “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). And it is the supreme example of love (1 Peter 2:21). Each picture is true. But beneath them all is substitution: he died in our place.

Colossians 2 joins two of these pictures. First a debt cancelled: the record against us was nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Then a victory won: the evil powers were disarmed and shamed, like captives led in a Roman triumph. The two are connected. Once our debt is paid, the accuser has nothing left to accuse us of.

Is substitution unjust?

Some teach that the cross was mainly a moral example, showing God’s love to move us to repentance. Others stress victory over evil powers. Some reject penal substitution entirely, calling it violent or unjust, as though an angry Father punished an unwilling Son.

The example and the victory are both biblical, but neither works without substitution. An example of love saves no one unless the death actually accomplished something for us. And Satan’s power over us rests on our guilt; when the guilt is removed, his accusations fail. Nor is substitution unjust. The Son was not an unwilling victim: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). Father, Son and Spirit were united in the plan. And the one who bore the penalty was God himself, in the person of the Son. The judge took the sentence.

For whom did Christ die? The Reformed answer, explained in the Doctrines of Grace study, is that his death actually secured the salvation of all the elect, while being sufficient for all and freely offered to all.

Every believer is Barabbas

Barabbas was a murderer and a rebel, guilty and condemned. The crowd chose him to be released, and Jesus was crucified instead (Mark 15:6–15). Barabbas walked free because another man took his place. Every believer is Barabbas.

A man who has heard about the cross all his life has always thought of it as something sad that happened to Jesus. Reading Isaiah 53 for the first time in a modern translation, he notices the pronouns: our transgressions, our iniquities, we are healed. He realises that the cross is not something that happened to Jesus. It is something Jesus did for him.

Can you explain in one sentence why Jesus died? Try using the words “for me” and “in my place”.

For reflection

Why could God not simply forgive sin without the cross? Read Isaiah 53 and underline every “we”, “our” and “us”: what do you notice? How would you answer someone who says penal substitution makes God cruel? How should the cross shape the way you think about your worst sins?

5.title: Risen, Ascended and Reigning
5.essay:
The story does not end at the tomb. “He is not here, for he has risen, as he said” (Matthew 28:6). On the third day Jesus rose bodily from the dead, and the course of history changed.

It happened

The tomb was empty, and even Jesus’ enemies did not deny it; they only tried to explain it away (Matthew 28:11–15). The risen Jesus appeared many times, to individuals and to groups — once to more than five hundred at the same time, most of whom were still alive when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:6). The disciples, who had fled in fear, became bold witnesses willing to suffer for their message.

First Corinthians 15 contains one of the earliest summaries of the Christian faith, which Paul had received and passed on: Christ died, was buried, was raised and appeared (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Paul lists witnesses by name and number, as if to say, “Go and ask them.” The resurrection is presented as history, open to checking. It is not a myth or a metaphor.

A real body

The risen Jesus was not a ghost. He invited the disciples to touch him, and he ate fish in front of them (Luke 24:39–43). His body was the same body, bearing the wounds, yet transformed and glorified, no longer subject to death. Our resurrection bodies will be like his (Philippians 3:21).

Everything hangs on Easter

The resurrection proves that Jesus is who he said he was: he “was declared to be the Son of God in power … by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4). It shows that the Father accepted his sacrifice: he “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). It defeats death. And it guarantees our own resurrection: Christ is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first sheaf of a harvest that is coming.

Paul faces the alternative squarely. If Christ has not been raised, faith is futile, sins are unforgiven, the dead are lost and Christians are the most pitiable people alive (1 Corinthians 15:17–19). Then comes the great reversal: “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Christianity stakes everything on one event, and that event happened.

The ascension

Forty days after his resurrection, Jesus was taken up into heaven before his disciples’ eyes (Acts 1:9). This was not his departure from the story but his coronation. He sat down at the right hand of God, the place of supreme authority, and from there he poured out the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:33). As the disciples stood staring at the sky, two angels told them that “this Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). The ascension means the disciples should not gaze upward but go outward, as witnesses to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8), until he returns.

The Son did not shed his human nature when he ascended. There is a man on the throne of the universe, and he is our brother. That is why he can sympathise with us, and why we will one day be with him bodily.

What Christ is doing now

He reigns over all things for the sake of his church (Ephesians 1:20–22). He builds his church through the preaching of the gospel. He is preparing a place for his people (John 14:2–3). And he intercedes for them. “Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died—more than that, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34). Each of those four facts answers a different accusation. Our security rests not on how well we are doing but on where Christ is and what he is doing.

Believers are united to Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:4–5). His resurrection life already works in us by the Spirit, giving us power to walk in newness of life, and one day it will raise our bodies. The risen Christ is not absent. He is present by his Spirit and active from his throne.

Breakfast on the beach

Peter had denied Jesus three times. After the resurrection, on a beach in Galilee, the risen Lord cooked him breakfast and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). The resurrection was not only a victory over death. It was the beginning of Peter’s restoration.

A widow stands at her husband’s graveside. She grieves deeply. But she believes that Christ is the firstfruits, and that her husband’s body, like a seed, will be raised. Her tears are real, but so is her hope. She does not “grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

What difference would it make to your life this week if the resurrection were not true? If the answer is “very little”, you may not yet have seen how much depends on it.

For reflection

Read 1 Corinthians 15:12–20. What would be lost if Christ had not been raised? How would you summarise the evidence for the resurrection to a sceptical friend? What difference does it make that a real man now sits on the throne of the universe? How does Christ’s intercession (Romans 8:34) speak to your fears or guilt?

6.title: He Will Come Again
6.essay:
The same Jesus who ascended will return. The New Testament speaks of the second coming again and again. It is the hope that sustained the early church, and the prayer with which the Bible ends: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

How he will come

Not secretly but visibly: “every eye will see him” (Revelation 1:7). Not as a humble baby but in glory: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). And not at a predictable date but suddenly: “concerning that day and hour no one knows” (Matthew 24:36). Jesus warned his followers not to be misled by those who claim to know.

What will happen

The dead will be raised, believers and unbelievers alike (John 5:28–29). Believers still alive will be transformed and caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Christ will judge the world: God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). The man who was judged at Pilate’s court will be the Judge of all. Then he will make all things new, and his people will live with him for ever on a renewed earth (Revelation 21:1–5).

Paul ended his speech in Athens with exactly this warning. God has overlooked ignorance in the past, but now “commands all people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30), because a day is fixed, the Judge is named, and God has given proof by raising him from the dead. The resurrection is not only a comfort; it is a summons.

Every knee will bow

Because Christ humbled himself, “God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2:9–10). Isaiah heard God say that every knee would bow to him (Isaiah 45:23); Paul applies those words to Jesus. Some will bow in joy, others in defeat, but every one will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, “to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

The order of events

Christians hold different views about the order of events at the end, which the End Times study sets out. The amillennial reading is the most faithful to Scripture: Christ reigns now, and at his single return there will be a general resurrection of the just and the unjust, the final judgment and the new creation. But all orthodox views agree on the central truth: Jesus will return bodily, visibly and gloriously to judge and to save.

Believers too will stand before Christ — not to be condemned, for “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), but to have their lives revealed and their faithfulness rewarded (2 Corinthians 5:10). The Judge is their Saviour.

How we wait

The second coming is not a puzzle for speculation but a motive for living. Paul joins Christ’s two comings in Titus 2. His first brought grace that trains us to live “self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age”, while we wait “for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:12–13) — a direct statement of his deity. So we wait with hope. We wait with holiness, because “everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure” (1 John 3:3). We wait with urgency, telling others while there is time. And we wait with comfort, for the Lord we long to see is the Lord who loves us.

The goal of history is not merely heaven but Christ. Paul’s longing was “to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23). The best thing about the new creation will be that he is there.

Encourage one another

The Thessalonian believers were grieving for members who had died before Christ returned. Paul did not give them a timetable. He gave them a hope: the dead in Christ will rise first, and we will all be with the Lord for ever. “Therefore encourage one another with these words” (1 Thessalonians 4:18).

A Christian notices that his thoughts about the future are full of retirement plans and worries about the economy and politics, and almost never of Christ’s return. He begins to end his evening prayers with “Come, Lord Jesus.” Over time his anxieties loosen. His future has a face.

If Christ returned today, would you be glad? What would you wish you had done differently?

For reflection

Why do you think the New Testament refuses to give a date for Christ’s return? How does 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 change the way Christians grieve? How should the hope of his return shape your week? Spend time praying “Come, Lord Jesus”: what feelings or fears does that prayer stir in you?
